{"rule":"Return this JSON object with the rule field unchanged and, in the text field, an original fictional passage of about 250 words that comes immediately AFTER the current text in the same invented story.","text":"For a moment, neither sister moved.

Then the stars stirred. They drifted across the floor like sparks shaken from a fire, gathering at the girl’s bare feet. She looked just as Mara remembered from the oldest photograph: a crooked smile, a freckle beneath one eye. But Mara had been six in that picture, and Elsie had been ten. Now they were both the age they had been on the night Elsie vanished.

“Mara,” Elsie whispered.

Mara stepped over the threshold. The room smelled of wet leaves and the cinnamon toast their mother used to burn on Sunday mornings. Behind her, the door groaned.

Their mother caught its edge. “Wait. If you cross, the door may not let you return.”

Elsie’s gaze flicked to the stone. “You brought it back.”

“I didn’t know what it was for,” Mara said.

“You did,” said their mother softly. “You just didn’t remember.”

At that, the scattered stars dimmed. A memory rose in Mara—not a picture, but a sensation: her small hand gripping Elsie’s sleeve, her own voice crying, Don’t leave me alone. Then a slammed door. Their mother’s face streaked with tears. Elsie’s furious promise to make them all forget.

The ache changed shape. It was still there, but it belonged to both of them now.

Elsie held out her hand. “I’m sorry I asked to disappear.”

Mara reached for her. Their fingers touched, and every star flared bright enough to turn the room into morning.

Behind them, their mother stepped across the threshold.

The red door swung shut by itself. Somewhere inside the stone, a tiny clear note rang—and this time, all three of them heard it."}
